newsitem.title: USA: U.S. refiners show spotty demand for foreign crude.
newsitem.headline: U.S. refiners show spotty demand for foreign crude.

text.p: U.S. refiners showed spotty demand for foreign crude Thursday amid weak margins and turnarounds at key Gulf Coast facilities, traders said.
The spread between benchmarks West Texas Intermediate and North Sea Brent was around $1.75-80 a barrel, giving sellers ample incentive to move transatlantic cargoes.
"There are some pockets of demand but on the flipside turnarounds are coming up," said one Northeast trader said.
One U.S. refiner was heard to have picked up a Brent cargo for mid-February arrival at March WTI minus 10 cents.
West African crudes, such as Qua Iboe and Bonny Light, seemed to be stirring up more interest, in part because most contain more gas oil than Brent does, traders said.

Latin American spot activity was subdued. Colombia's state owned Ecopetrol was heard to have sold a cargo of Cano Limon for loading in mid-February, possibly into neighboring Peru, for an unconfirmed discount of $1.30-35 a barrel to March WTI fob.
"That was an outstanding sale if it's true," one trader said.
The Colombian company is also offering a Vasconia cargo for the end of January, they said.
A private equity producer still has a Cusiana cargo available for the end of January, traders said.
In the U.S. aftermarket, a series of partial paper March Brent cargoes changed hands at $23.94 and $23.96 a barrel, compared to the London close of $24.02.
Brent Feb/March changed hands twice at 53 and once at 55 cents, down one to three cents from the IPE settlement.
